content: When co-administered with ritonavir and other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV infection in treatment-naïve or treatment-experienced patients without darunavir resistance-associated substitutions, the recommended dose is 800 mg of darunavir plus 100 mg of ritonavir taken orally once daily with food. For treatment-experienced patients with at least one darunavir resistance-associated mutation or when genotyping is not available, the recommended dose is 600 mg of darunavir plus 100 mg of ritonavir taken orally every 12 hours with food. In treatment-experienced patients, it is recommended to assess the drug susceptibility of the HIV-1 virus through treatment history, genotypic, and/or phenotypic testing. Laboratory testing, such as serum liver biochemistry, should be obtained before initiating darunavir therapy. Patients with underlying chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or elevated pretreatment liver enzymes should be closely monitored for elevated transaminases, particularly during the first several months of treatment. The safety and efficacy of darunavir co-administered with ritonavir and other antiretroviral agents have not been established in children under 3 years of age or weighing ≤10 kg. Darunavir must be taken with food to ensure proper absorption. Darunavir is contraindicated with certain medications due to its effects on hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism, which can lead to significant drug interactions. These include: 1. Alfuzosin: Darunavir increases alfuzosin levels, potentially causing serious or life-threatening reactions. 2. Aprepitant: Darunavir increases aprepitant levels, leading to contraindication. 3. Carbamazepine: Co-administration decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance development. 4. Cobicistat: Darunavir increases cobicistat levels significantly, contraindicating their use together. 5. Conivaptan: Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated. 6. Dihydroergotamine (intranasal): Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 7. Dronedarone: Darunavir increases dronedarone levels, contraindicating use. 8. Elbasvir/Grazoprevir: Darunavir increases their levels, raising the risk of ALT elevations. 9. Eliglustat: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir are contraindicated with eliglustat in poor or intermediate metabolizers. 10. Elvitegravir/Cobicistat/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir DF: This combination is a complete HIV regimen and should not be co-administered with other antiretrovirals. 11. Ergoloid Mesylates: Darunavir increases their levels, contraindicating use. 12. Ergonovine: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 13. Finerinone: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 14. Flibanserin: Co-administration with moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated due to risks of severe hypotension or syncope. 15. Fosaprepitant: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 16. Gepirone: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 17. Irinotecan/Irinotecan Liposomal: Darunavir increases their levels, contraindicating use. 18. Isavuconazonium Sulfate: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 19. Ivabradine: Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated. 20. Lomitapide: Darunavir significantly increases its levels, contraindicating use. 21. Lonafarnib: Co-administration with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated. 22. Lovastatin: Darunavir increases its levels, raising the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. 23. Lurasidone: Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated. 24. Mavacamten: Darunavir increases its levels, potentially causing heart failure due to systolic dysfunction. 25. Methylergonovine: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 26. Naloxegol: Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated due to the risk of opioid withdrawal symptoms. 27. Pacritinib: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 28. Phenobarbital: Co-administration decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance development. 29. Phenytoin: Co-administration decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance development. 30. Pimozide: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 31. Ranolazine: Darunavir increases its levels, potentially causing serious or life-threatening reactions. 32. Regorafenib: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir increase regorafenib levels while decreasing exposure to its active metabolites. 33. Rifampin: Co-administration decreases darunavir levels, risking loss of antiviral efficacy and resistance development. 34. Salmeterol: Darunavir increases its levels, raising the risk of toxicity. 35. Simvastatin: Darunavir increases its levels, raising the risk of rhabdomyolysis. 36. St. John’s Wort: Co-administration decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance development. 37. Triazolam/Midazolam (oral): Darunavir significantly increases their levels, potentially causing prolonged sedation or respiratory depression. 38. Venetoclax: Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated during the initial ramp-up phase. 39. Voclosporin: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use. 40. Acalabrutinib: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir. If necessary, temporarily interrupt acalabrutinib treatment. 41. Adagrasib: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir until steady-state concentrations are reached. 42. Ado-Trastuzumab Emtansine: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir may increase DM1 exposure and toxicity. 43. Afatinib: Darunavir increases its levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Reduce the afatinib dose if not tolerated. 44. Apalutamide: Co-administration decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure. Avoid or substitute another drug. 45. Apixaban: Avoid co-administration with strong dual inhibitors of CYP3A4 and P-gp. 46. Atidarsagene Autotemcel: Antiretroviral medications may interfere with its manufacturing. Avoid ARTs for at least one month before cell mobilization. 47. Avanafil: Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir is contraindicated due to risks of severe adverse events. 48. Avapritinib: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir. 49. Axitinib: If co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the axitinib dose by 50%. 50. Bedaquiline: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like darunavir for more than 14 consecutive days unless the benefit outweighs the risk. 51. Betibeglogene Autotemcel: Avoid antiretroviral medications for at least one month before mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed. 52. Bosentan: Co-administration decreases darunavir levels. Adjust bosentan dosing as needed. 53. Bosutinib: Darunavir increases its levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 54. Brigatinib: If co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the brigatinib dose by 50%. 55. Bromocriptine: Darunavir increases its levels. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 56. Cabergoline: Darunavir increases its levels, contraindicating use.
